name: Chapli Kabab
description: Pashtun-style chapli kababs made with seasoned beef mince, crushed coriander and cumin, herbs and tomato, shaped thin and shallow-fried until browned and cooked through.
ingredients: 750 g beef mince with some fat
1 medium tomato, finely chopped and excess juice removed
1 small onion, finely chopped and squeezed of excess moisture
1 tsp red chili flakes or to taste
method: Combine the beef mince with the squeezed onion, green chillies, fresh coriander, crushed coriander seeds, cumin, chilli flakes, maize flour, egg and salt. Mix until the seasonings are evenly distributed and the mince begins to hold together.
Fold in the finely chopped, well-drained tomato shortly before shaping; removing excess tomato and onion moisture helps prevent the mixture from becoming loose.
With damp hands, form broad, relatively thin patties of even thickness. If they feel too soft to handle cleanly, chill the shaped or mixed kababs briefly before frying.
Heat a shallow layer of oil over medium heat. Add the kababs in batches with space between them so the pan temperature does not drop sharply.
Let the first side develop a firm browned crust before turning. Cook the second side until browned and make sure the centre is fully cooked, using a reliable doneness check for minced meat.
Drain briefly so excess surface oil runs off, then serve hot with chutney, naan, sliced onion or salad.
tips: Remove excess moisture from onion and tomato to help the kababs hold together.
Make the patties relatively thin so the centre cooks before the exterior burns.
storage: Cool cooked kababs promptly and refrigerate covered. Reheat the portion you plan to eat until thoroughly hot.
image_alt: Pakistani chapli kabab with browned flat minced-meat patties served as a Pashtun-style kebab dish
image_caption: Traditional chapli kabab photographed as a Pashtun-style minced-meat kebab dish.
technique: Chapli kabab is shaped flatter than seekh kabab so a broad surface can brown while the centre stays juicy. Keep tomato and other wet ingredients controlled, shape immediately before frying, and use enough heat to brown without burning the spices.
doneness_cues: The mixture should feel moist and cohesive but should not release a puddle of water.
Patties should be thin and broad with rough edges rather than thick burger-like discs.
The first side should develop a deep brown crust before turning.
The centre must be fully cooked while the edges remain crisp rather than hard.
mistakes: Adding very juicy tomato too early and letting the mixture sit until it becomes wet.
Shaping thick patties that stay dense in the centre.
Frying on heat so high that coriander and exterior spices burn before the meat cooks.
Pressing cooked kababs repeatedly with a spatula and squeezing out juices.
substitutions: Use firm tomato and remove excessive watery seed pulp if the mixture already feels loose.
The chilli level can be reduced while keeping crushed coriander and cumin for the characteristic aromatic profile.
If your mince is unusually wet, chill the mixed batch before shaping rather than adding large amounts of dry filler.
reheating: Warm chapli kababs in a dry or lightly greased pan over medium-low heat, covered briefly if needed. Reheat only until hot so the centre stays moist.

faqs.question: Why does chapli kabab break while frying?
faqs.answer: Excess moisture, a warm soft mixture or turning before the first side sets are common causes. Chill the mixture and cook a small test patty first.

faqs.question: Why are my chapli kababs hard?
faqs.answer: They may be too thick, too lean, overmixed or overcooked. Keep them thin and stop cooking once the centre is done.

faqs.question: Can I prepare the mixture ahead?
faqs.answer: You can prepare much of it ahead, but very wet ingredients such as chopped tomato are better added close to shaping so they do not loosen the mixture.
